lead: This unit turns Newton's laws into working equations for a moving fluid. You stop following a fixed lump of water and start watching a fixed region of space, then apply energy, momentum and viscosity inside it. After this unit you can find a discharge from a pressure difference, the force on a pipe bend, the velocity profile between two plates, and say what changes when a gas flows fast enough to compress.
about: Chapter 3.1 gives the Reynolds transport theorem, the bridge from a moving system to a fixed control volume. Chapter 3.2 applies it along a streamline to get Euler's equation, and 3.3 integrates that into Bernoulli's equation with its assumptions and head form. Chapter 3.4 uses Bernoulli plus continuity for the venturimeter, orificemeter and pitot tube, and 3.5 does the same for orifices, mouthpieces, notches and weirs with their coefficients. Chapter 3.6 returns to the control volume for linear and angular momentum, so forces and torques can be found where energy alone is not enough. Chapter 3.7 shrinks the control volume to a point and adds viscosity, giving the Navier-Stokes equations and a few exact solutions. Chapter 3.8 adds density change, Mach number and choking.

chapters.idea: The rate of change of a property of a fixed mass of fluid equals the rate of change inside a chosen control volume plus the net rate carried out across its surface.
chapters.depth: State the theorem for an extensive property B with intensive value b = B/m: dB/dt = ∂/∂t ∫ρb dV + ∫ρb(V·n)dA. Define system (a fixed mass), control volume (a region in space), control surface, extensive vs intensive, and the outward normal n. Explain why the theorem exists: the laws of mechanics are written for a fixed mass, but a pipe, nozzle or pump is easier to draw as a fixed region. Give the steady form and the special cases b = 1 (mass, which gives continuity), b = V (momentum), b = r × V (angular momentum) and b = e (energy). Some syllabi call it the Reynolds transport equation, or treat it as Leibniz's rule for a moving volume. Mention the moving-control-volume form in one line only.

figure.title: From system to control volume
figure.aria: A block diagram splitting the rate of change of a system property into an inside-the-control-volume term and a net outward flux term, which together form the Reynolds transport theorem.

chapters.example: Water flows steadily through a fixed control volume. At inlet section 1 the area is 0.01 m² and the velocity is 2 m/s. At outlet section 2 the area is 0.02 m². Density is 1000 kg/m³. Find the net rate of momentum leaving the control volume and the force on the fluid. Discharge Q = A₁V₁ = 0.01 × 2 = 0.02 m³/s. By continuity V₂ = Q/A₂ = 0.02/0.02 = 1 m/s. The flow is steady, so the volume term is zero. Momentum flux out = ρQ(V₂ − V₁) = 1000 × 0.02 × (1 − 2) = −20 N. Momentum leaves at 20 N in the negative direction, so the force on the fluid is 20 N pointing upstream.
chapters.trap: Using the acceleration of the system instead of the surface flux integral. Forgetting that n points outward, so an inflow carries a negative sign. Using the steady form while the amount inside the control volume is changing, as in a tank being filled.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: system and control volume, continuity equation, streamlines.
chapters.leave: The differential form is derived in 3.7. Pipe friction and energy lines are Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Along one streamline of an inviscid fluid, the pressure force and gravity on a small element produce exactly the acceleration of that element.
chapters.depth: Derive from F = ma on a cylindrical element of length ds, cross-section dA, inclined at angle θ to the horizontal: p dA − (p + dp) dA − ρg dA ds cos θ = ρ dA ds (dV/dt), then use dV/dt = V dV/ds. Result: dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0. Define streamline, steady flow, inviscid (no shear stress), θ, and dz = ds sin θ. Show three forms: along a streamline; for a horizontal streamline, dp/ds = −ρV dV/ds; and normal to a streamline, dp/dn = ρV²/r with r the radius of curvature, which only a few syllabi include. List the assumptions: steady, inviscid, along a streamline, constant density only for the integrated form.

figure.title: Forces on an element along a streamline
figure.aria: A flowchart that starts with a fluid element on a streamline, resolves pressure and weight forces, equates them to mass times acceleration, and ends with the Euler equation.

chapters.example: Water flows along a horizontal streamline. The velocity rises from 2 m/s to 3 m/s over a distance of 0.5 m. Density is 1000 kg/m³. Find the pressure gradient and the pressure change over that distance. For a horizontal streamline dp/ds = −ρV dV/ds. Take the mean velocity V = 2.5 m/s and dV/ds = (3 − 2)/0.5 = 2 s⁻¹. Then dp/ds = −1000 × 2.5 × 2 = −5000 Pa/m. Over 0.5 m the pressure falls by 5000 × 0.5 = 2500 Pa.
chapters.trap: Applying Euler across streamlines in a curved or rotational flow. Dropping the gravity term on a sloping streamline. Using it where viscosity acts or where a pump sits between the two points.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: streamlines, acceleration of a fluid particle. Unit 1: pressure and Newton's law of viscosity.
chapters.leave: The integration to Bernoulli is 3.3. Real losses and pumps come in Unit 4 and Unit 7.

chapters.idea: For steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, pressure head plus elevation head plus velocity head stays constant.
chapters.depth: Integrate Euler at constant density: p/γ + z + V²/2g = constant, every term in metres of the flowing fluid. Define γ = ρg, datum for z, piezometric head p/γ + z, velocity head V²/2g, total head, and stagnation pressure p + ρV²/2. Give the derivation from Euler and the parallel derivation from the steady energy equation. State the assumptions plainly: steady, incompressible, inviscid, along a streamline, no work device between the two points, continuous flow. Work through Torricelli's result V = √(2gh) for a tank, the siphon, and the modified equation with a pump head h_p and a loss h_L (cross-reference Unit 4). Mention that the energy line and hydraulic gradient line are drawn in Unit 4, not here.

figure.aria: A graph along a converging horizontal pipe where the pressure head falls as the velocity head rises by the same amount, keeping the total head fixed at 5 metres.

chapters.example: Water flows at 0.05 m³/s through a pipe of 15 cm diameter at a pressure of 150 kPa gauge. The pipe then rises 4 m and narrows to 10 cm diameter. Losses are neglected. Find the pressure at the upper section. A₁ = π×0.075² = 0.01767 m², so V₁ = 0.05/0.01767 = 2.83 m/s. A₂ = π×0.05² = 0.007854 m², so V₂ = 0.05/0.007854 = 6.37 m/s. Bernoulli from 1 to 2: p₂ = p₁ + ρg(z₁ − z₂) + ρ(V₁² − V₂²)/2. Substitute: p₂ = 150000 − 1000×9.81×4 + 500×(8.01 − 40.53) = 150000 − 39240 − 16260 = 94,500 Pa, that is about 94.5 kPa gauge.
chapters.trap: Applying one Bernoulli equation across a pump, a turbine or a loss without adding that head term. Forgetting that the pressure in the equation is usually gauge. Assuming it holds across streamlines in a rotational flow such as a forced vortex.
chapters.leave: Losses, energy line and hydraulic gradient line belong to Unit 4. Pump and turbine heads belong to Units 6 and 7. The compressible energy equation is 3.8.

chapters.idea: A venturimeter, an orificemeter and a pitot tube all find velocity or discharge from one measured pressure difference, using Bernoulli plus continuity, and differ only in which area is known.
chapters.depth: Venturimeter: converging cone, throat, diverging cone; derive Q = Cd A₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁² − A₂²), where h is the head difference in metres of the flowing liquid. Give the manometer conversion h = x(S_m/S − 1) for a manometer liquid of specific gravity S_m in a pipe carrying liquid of specific gravity S. Typical Cd is 0.95 to 0.98. Orificemeter: Q = Cd A₀√(2gh)/√(1 − (A₀/A₁)²), Cd about 0.6, with the vena contracta explaining the larger loss. Pitot tube: stagnation pressure, V = √(2gh) at a point, coefficient about 0.98, and the fact that a pitot reading in a pipe is a local velocity, not the mean. Mention the pitot-static tube and its U-tube manometer.

figure.title: Deriving the venturimeter formula
figure.aria: A step-by-step flowchart from inlet section to throat, through Bernoulli and continuity and the manometer reading, ending in the venturimeter discharge formula.

chapters.example: A venturimeter with a pipe diameter of 25 cm and a throat diameter of 12.5 cm carries water. The mercury manometer reads 20 cm and Cd = 0.98. Find the discharge. A₁ = π×0.125² = 0.04909 m². A₂ = π×0.0625² = 0.01227 m². Head of water h = x(S_m/S − 1) = 0.20×(13.6 − 1) = 2.52 m. √(2gh) = √(2×9.81×2.52) = 7.03 m/s. Then Q = Cd A₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁² − A₂²) = 0.98 × 0.04909 × 0.01227 × 7.03 / √(0.002410 − 0.0001506) = 0.004152/0.04753 = 0.0873 m³/s, about 87 L/s.
chapters.trap: Using the throat area alone instead of the combined A₁A₂/√(A₁² − A₂²) term. Forgetting the manometer factor and taking x itself as the head. Treating a pitot tube reading as the mean velocity when it is the velocity at one point.
chapters.leave: Orifice flow from a tank and flow over weirs are 3.5. The rotameter and other variable-area meters are usually outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Flow through a hole or over a notch follows Bernoulli, so the ideal discharge is known and only one coefficient is needed, and that coefficient splits into contraction and velocity.
chapters.depth: Orifice: small and large, sharp-edged; vena contracta; Cc = area of jet / area of hole, about 0.62; Cv = actual/theoretical velocity, about 0.98; Cd = Cc Cv, about 0.60 to 0.62. Head is measured above the centre of the orifice. Mouthpiece: internal and external, external cylindrical Cd about 0.82, Borda mouthpiece Cd about 0.5 in one line. Notches and weirs: rectangular Q = (2/3)Cd L√(2g)H^{3/2}; triangular or V-notch Q = (8/15)Cd√(2g)tan(θ/2)H^{5/2}; name the trapezoidal and Cipolletti weir in one line. End contraction: effective length L − 0.1nH for n contractions. Velocity of approach: replace H by H + h_a, where h_a = V_a²/2g and V_a is the approach velocity. Include the Francis formula for a suppressed weir.

figure.aria: A tree of flow openings: an orifice, a mouthpiece, a notch and a weir, each splitting into its common types with a short label on the edge.

chapters.example: A rectangular sharp-crested weir with no end contractions has a crest length of 3 m and carries water with a head of 0.4 m over the crest. Take Cd = 0.62 and neglect the velocity of approach. Find the discharge. Q = (2/3)Cd L√(2g)H^{3/2}. √(2×9.81) = 4.43 m^0.5/s. H^{3/2} = 0.4^{3/2} = 0.253. So Q = 0.6667 × 0.62 × 3 × 4.43 × 0.253 = 1.39 m³/s. With one end contraction the effective length would be 3 − 0.1×1×0.4 = 2.96 m, giving about 1.37 m³/s.
chapters.trap: Measuring the head close to the crest instead of well upstream, or from the wrong line. Forgetting the end-contraction term 0.1nH, or the velocity of approach. Using one coefficient, such as the orifice Cd, for a weir as well.
chapters.leave: The venturimeter and pitot tube are 3.4. Open channel uniform flow by Chezy or Manning is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: The force of a fluid on a bend, vane or nozzle equals the rate at which momentum leaves minus the rate at which it enters, plus the pressure forces on the control surface, and the same control volume with a moment arm gives torque.
chapters.depth: Take the Reynolds transport theorem with b = V: ΣF = ∂/∂t∫ρV dV + ∫ρV(V·n)dA. Steady form: ΣF = ṁ(V₂ − V₁), with ṁ = ρQ. Define control volume, pressure force, body force, and the two sign viewpoints: force on the fluid and force on the boundary. Do the reducing bend in a horizontal plane, a nozzle, a sudden enlargement, and the link to the momentum check on a pitot tube. Angular form: ΣT = ṁ(r₂ × V₂ − r₁ × V₁), stated with one worked step for a lawn sprinkler or a rotating arm. Mention the accelerating control volume, which only a few syllabi ask for.

figure.title: Forces on a pipe bend
figure.aria: A block diagram of a control volume around a pipe bend, combining inlet and outlet momentum fluxes with the pressure force to give the force on the fluid and then the equal and opposite force on the bend.

chapters.example: Water flows at 0.1 m³/s through a horizontal 90° reducing bend. The inlet diameter is 20 cm and the outlet diameter is 10 cm. The outlet discharges to atmosphere. Neglect losses and find the force on the bend. A₁ = 0.03142 m², V₁ = 3.18 m/s. A₂ = 0.007854 m², V₂ = 12.73 m/s. Bernoulli from 1 to 2 with p₂ = 0 gives p₁ = ρ(V₂² − V₁²)/2 = 500×(162.1 − 10.1) = 76,000 Pa. x-direction: Fx(wall on fluid) + p₁A₁ = ρQ(0 − V₁) = 1000×0.1×(−3.18) = −318 N, so Fx = −318 − 76,000×0.03142 = −318 − 2388 = −2706 N. y-direction: Fy = ρQ(V₂ − 0) = 1273 N. Force of water on the bend is (2706, −1273) N, magnitude 2990 N, nearly 3 kN, at about 25° below the inlet axis.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the pressure forces at inlet and outlet. Mixing the force on the fluid with the force on the bend and losing a sign. Forgetting the momentum flux in the second direction when the bend turns the flow.
chapters.prereq: 3.1: Reynolds transport theorem. Unit 2: continuity equation.
chapters.leave: Impact of jets on vanes and the Euler turbomachine torque belong to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Applying Newton's second law to a differential element and including viscous shear gives the Navier-Stokes equations, and a few simple flows can be solved exactly by dropping the terms that vanish.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities expect the full derivation, so keep it short. Cover the stress on a fluid element (pressure plus viscous stress) and the general equation ρ(∂V/∂t + V·∇V) = −∇p + ρg + μ∇²V, with ∇·V = 0 for incompressible flow. Name each term: local, convective, pressure, gravity, viscous. State that the equations are nonlinear and have no general solution. Exact solutions: plane Couette flow u = Uy/h; plane Poiseuille flow u = (1/2μ)(−dp/dx)(hy − y²); Hagen-Poiseuille in a circular pipe, result only, cross-referenced to Unit 4; Stokes flow past a sphere in one line. Explain fully developed flow and why ∂u/∂x = 0 forces v = 0 by continuity.

figure.aria: A graph of velocity profiles between parallel plates: a parabola for pressure-driven flow with its peak at mid-gap, and a straight line for flow driven by a moving upper plate.

chapters.example: Oil of viscosity 0.05 Pa·s flows steadily and fully developed between two fixed parallel plates 5 mm apart. The pressure gradient is 1200 Pa per metre and the flow is laminar. Find the maximum velocity, the mean velocity and the discharge per metre width. u_max = (−dp/dx)h²/(8μ) = 1200 × (0.005)²/(8 × 0.05) = 0.03/0.4 = 0.075 m/s. For this profile the mean is two-thirds of the maximum, so mean = 0.05 m/s. Discharge per metre width = 0.05 × 0.005 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s per metre.
chapters.trap: Dropping terms without saying why. Losing the sign of dp/dx so the profile comes out negative. Confusing maximum and mean velocity: the mean is two-thirds of the maximum between plates and one-half of the maximum in a pipe.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Newton's law of viscosity. Unit 2: continuity, velocity field. 3.6: momentum for a control volume.
chapters.leave: Pipe friction factor, Moody chart and losses are Unit 4. Boundary layers and separation are Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Above a Mach number of about 0.3 the density of a gas changes enough that the incompressible equations fail, and a set of relations in Mach number and γ takes over.
chapters.depth: Define Mach number M = V/c, speed of sound c = √(γRT), γ = cp/cv, and R = 287 J/(kg·K) for air. Give stagnation properties T₀ = T(1 + (γ−1)M²/2) and p₀/p = (1 + (γ−1)M²/2)^{γ/(γ−1)}, which is 3.5 for air. Give the steady energy equation for adiabatic flow, h₀ constant. Cover the area-velocity relation dA/A = (M² − 1)dV/V, the converging nozzle with choking at M = 1 in the throat, the converging-diverging or de Laval nozzle, and the Mach cone for M > 1 in one line. State the incompressible limit M < 0.3. This is an introduction; only a few universities examine it with numbers.

figure.aria: A graph of the area ratio A over A-star against Mach number for air: it falls to exactly 1 at Mach 1 and rises again on both the subsonic and the supersonic side.

chapters.example: Air with γ = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg·K) is at 300 K and flows at Mach 2. Find the speed of sound, the flow speed and the stagnation temperature. Also find the ratio p₀/p. c = √(γRT) = √(1.4 × 287 × 300) = √120540 = 347 m/s. Flow speed V = M c = 2 × 347 = 694 m/s. Stagnation temperature T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²) = 300 × (1 + 0.8) = 540 K. Pressure ratio p₀/p = 1.8^{3.5} = 7.83, so the stagnation pressure is 7.83 times the static pressure.
chapters.trap: Putting the static temperature or pressure into a formula that asks for the stagnation value. Using incompressible Bernoulli at Mach 2. Forgetting that the exponent 3.5 holds only for γ = 1.4, as for air.
chapters.prereq: 3.3: Bernoulli and the energy equation. Unit 1: density and compressibility.
chapters.leave: Flow with friction or heat transfer (Fanno and Rayleigh flow) and normal shocks are outside this unit. The static temperature rise in a compressor belongs with pumps and compressors.

links: the theorem applied to momentum along a streamline gives Euler
integrating Euler at constant density gives Bernoulli
Bernoulli plus continuity gives the meter formulas
Bernoulli through a hole gives orifice and weir discharge
the theorem with b = V gives the momentum equation
energy finds the pressure, momentum finds the force
momentum on a shrinking control volume gives Navier-Stokes
the same equations with variable density lead to compressible flow
the energy equation gives stagnation temperature
